Limited to occasional (but very fulfilling) conversations with my small group of close friends who now live in various far off places. This made me lonely at first, but it also put the fact that social interaction is a lot like an addictive, and not always productive, drug, into perspective, and gave me the opportunity to learn exactly what I was getting from social interaction, what was positive and negative about that, and how to enjoy my time without having to be around other people. At this point I think the mental place that I've arrived at through learning to enjoy solitude is really valuable and I'm glad I found it. Solitude also makes your social interactions a lot more potent when they do come around. You have a bunch of things to talk about, you can appreciate your friends for their uniqueness and really see why you like them, or realize that maybe you don't actually like some people. It brings everything into sharper relief.

Learning to be alone opens up new dimensions of experiencing life. If you're never alone, experiencing and thinking for yourself, without social considerations, you never really get to know yourself or sort out your own perspective.
